Its response stated that microscopic discectomy and endoscopic discectomy are associated with better outcomes and fewer complications compared to open discectomy. A randomized control study published in 2019 found that hospital stay, bone loss, estimated blood loss, and postoperative complications were all lower in microdiscectomy compared to open discectomy for patients with high level lumbar disc prolapse [ ]. Although this is in line with ChatGPT’s response, the generalizability of this study is limited due to its small sample size. A meta-analysis from 2022 analyzing pooled randomized control trials found that overall complication rates for full endoscopic lumbar discectomy (FELD) was 5.5% while complications for open discectomy/microdiscectomy was 10.4% [ ]. This suggests that patients that received FELD procedures have a lower risk ration for overall complications (risk ratio [RR], 0.55; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.31–0.98) [ ]. While this is also in line with ChatGPT’s response, there was no significant difference regarding overall complications between the 2 cohorts. Interestingly, there was a difference in heterogeneous complication results suggesting that patients who receive FELD procedures to treat lumbar disc herniation with radiculopathy are at greater risk for dysesthesia (RR, 3.70; 95% CI, 1.54–8.89), residual fragment (RR, 5.29; 95% CI, 2.67–10.45), and revision surgeries (RR, 1.53; 95% CI, 1.12–2.08) [ ]. Overall, the literature regarding complications and outcomes between surgical procedures is complex and future studies need to be performed before definitive statements can be made. The NASS 2012 guidelines for lumbar disc herniation with radiculopathy give no recommendation or have abstained from commenting on the impact of the site-of-service chosen for surgical management on the value of treatment. ChatGPT, however, posits the notion that the chosen site-of-service can affect the value of treatment and defines the latter as “clinical outcomes” and “cost-effectiveness.” Despite the lack of evidence that NASS used to justify not commenting on the topic, ChatGPT suggested that hospitals tend to lead to higher costs compared to outpatient settings for the surgical management of this condition. A 2021 study concluded that outpatient lumbar discectomy (a type of surgical management for lumbar herniation) has a higher cost-effectiveness compared to its inpatient counterpart [ ]. While this study may support ChatGPT’s conclusions regarding cost-effectiveness, this study is not generalizable due to its low sample size (N=40). Other studies have found that procedures like lumbar microdiscectomy can have reduced costs in the ambulatory setting compared to the hospital associated outpatient centers in patient populations insured with both Medicare and commercial insurances [ ]. This evidence may suggest benefits in terms of cost-effectiveness for the surgical management of this spinal condition which is in line with ChatGPT’s response. However, these findings may not be generalizable and the patient population for which these findings may be true is a very specific one. The study found that relatively healthier populations would benefit more from outpatient surgery [ ]. It should be emphasized that ChatGPT-3.5 is primarily a language model trained on a broad spectrum of general knowledge rather than specialized medical information [ , ], which might account for some of the observed variances when compared to NASS guidelines. However, given ChatGPT’s ease of access and increasing usage, it was crucial to evaluate its precision in delivering medically accurate information to ensure that patients are receiving reliable data. The latest version of ChatGPT-4, which benefits from training on a more extensive dataset updated as of 2023, has shown potential for improved performance in specialized areas including medical queries. This was evident in a recent comparative study between ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4, specifically focusing on their outputs related to thromboembolic prophylaxis in spinal surgery [ ]. In our study, however, there were no statistically significant differences between the responses provided by ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4 which brings into question ChatGPT-4’s ability to perform better at domain specific information. Given this discrepancy, it’s crucial to recognize that ChatGPT is an evolving platform and as such, each new version should undergo ongoing validation to analyze its accuracy and reliability so as to ensure that patients are receiving accurate information. The evolution from ChatGPT-3.5 to GPT-4 represents a significant milestone in the development of advanced language models by OpenAI. ChatGPT-3.5, released in early 2022, was an iteration based on the GPT-3 architecture and boasted around 6 billion parameters. This version was trained on diverse internet text up to 2021, enabling it to generate more contextually relevant and nuanced responses in conversational AI applications. undergo ongoing validation to analyze its accuracy and reliability so as to ensure that patients are receiving accurate information. The evolution from ChatGPT-3.5 to GPT-4 represents a significant milestone in the development of advanced language models by OpenAI. ChatGPT-3.5, released in early 2022, was an iteration based on the GPT-3 architecture and boasted around 6 billion parameters. This version was trained on diverse internet text up to 2021, enabling it to generate more contextually relevant and nuanced responses in conversational AI applications. While the exact number of parameters for GPT-4 was not publicly disclosed, it significantly exceeded the 175 billion, and was trained on a dataset inclusive of text and other data types up to the year 2022, enhancing its understanding and generation capabilities across a wider range of contexts and languages [ ]. Additionally, OpenAI unveiled ChatGPT-4 Turbo on November 6, 2023, featuring a dataset current as of April 2023. This latest iteration introduces the capability to develop tailored models. With this enhancement, it’s possible to input extensive volumes of specialized data for targeted training, leading to more refined and precise outputs [ ]. This advancement holds particular significance in medical applications. By feeding the model the latest medical data, specialized in certain areas of healthcare, it’s feasible to create a model that provides more accurate and up-to-date medical information. Before the launch of ChatGPT Turbo-4, various teams had initiated the development of LLMs specifically tailored for the healthcare sector. A prominent example is Med-LLama, introduced in February 2023. This model builds upon the large language model meta-AI (LLaMA) framework, incorporating over 100,000 anonymized conversations between patients and doctors from an online medical consultation service. Med-LLaMA also integrates current information from online resources, along with various offline medical databases. This integration significantly enhances the model’s medical expertise and the precision of its advice [ ]. Released in 2023, PMC-LLaMA is another significant contribution to the field of medical-specific domain LLMs. As an open-source model, it has undergone extensive refinement, having been fine-tuned with an extensive dataset of 4.8 million biomedical academic papers. This enhancement ensures that both patients and physicians can easily access precise medical knowledge, streamlining the information flow in healthcare settings [ ]. It is important to note that literature is lacking on the specific utilization of Med-LLaMA and PMC-LLaMA, highlighting the importance of conduction analyses of these platforms to ensure their safety in the medical setting. In the medical field, ChatGPT and other LLMs are being explored for various applications. A systematic review conducted following investigated ChatGPT’s utility in healthcare education, research, and practice. This review, which included 60 records, identified several benefits of ChatGPT: improved scientific writing, research equity, efficiency in analyzing datasets, utility in drug discovery, streamlining healthcare workflows, cost-saving, enhancing personalized medicine, and improving health literacy. It also found ChatGPT useful in healthcare education for promoting personalized learning and critical thinking. However, 96.7% of the records cited concerns, including ethical and legal issues, risk of bias, plagiarism, inaccurate content, and cybersecurity risks [ ]. The review emphasized the need for cautious adoption of ChatGPT in healthcare, highlighting its potential to induce paradigm shifts in the field but also the necessity of addressing its limitations. In another recent study evaluating the diagnostic capabilities of ChatGPT-4, in neuroradiology, 100 cases from the American Journal of Neuroradiology were analyzed. ChatGPT’s diagnoses, based on patients’ medical histories and imaging findings, were compared with published ground truths, achieving an overall accuracy rate of 50%. These findings highlight the potential and limitations of ChatGPT in neuroradiological applications, further emphasizing its varied accuracy depending on specific medical conditions [ ]. A recent literature review investigating the use of AI and machine learning in spine surgery, encompassing 46 studies, discovered that AI models achieved an accuracy rate of 74.9%. These models were particularly effective in patient selection, estimating costs, and predicting the length of hospital stays. Additionally, they demonstrated great performance in forecasting functional outcomes and the likelihood of postoperative mortality [ ]. This underscores the importance of healthcare personnel to familiarize themselves with AI as a tool to potentially improve patient outcomes. A significant difficulty in employing ChatGPT and comparable LLMs is their inclination to provide definitive answers to questions, even when a lack of agreement would be more fitting. This phenomenon, called artificial hallucination, happens when these models create plausible yet unsupported statements that are not backed by their training data [ ]. ChatGPT-4 was previously found to avoid this issue of fabricated reference production [ ], however, in our study we found that ChatGPT-4 still backed up some of its claims by fabricating studies. In response to queries about references, ChatGPT-4 clarified that it lacked the capability to cite specific references and instead generated responses based on the information it was trained on. Nevertheless, there were instances where

even when a lack of agreement would be more fitting. This phenomenon, called artificial hallucination, happens when these models create plausible yet unsupported statements that are not backed by their training data [ ]. ChatGPT-4 was previously found to avoid this issue of fabricated reference production [ ], however, in our study we found that ChatGPT-4 still backed up some of its claims by fabricating studies. In response to queries about references, ChatGPT-4 clarified that it lacked the capability to cite specific references and instead generated responses based on the information it was trained on. Nevertheless, there were instances where ChatGPT-4 did indeed mention valid studies, which were subsequently verified by reviewers. Despite an improved likelihood of providing accurate references, ChatGPT-4 was not immune to occasional instances of generating erroneous information, reflecting the phenomenon of artificial hallucinations. It is of considerable significance to highlight that the generation of medically pertinent queries is critical in acquiring informative clinical responses from ChatGPT. Although healthcare professionals and individuals with a healthcare-related background possess the necessary expertise to effectively generate such queries, nonexperts may encounter difficulties in doing so when attempting to obtain answers. Nonexperts may pose questions in an inappropriate or imprecise manner, resulting in inadequate responses from ChatGPT if they seek to substitute a medical consultation with a search query. As a result, it is imperative to exercise caution while utilizing ChatGPT and not to regard it as a substitute for medical consultations. Our study presented some noteworthy limitations. Firstly, the NASS guidelines for lumbar disc herniation with radiculopathy have not been updated since 2012. It is probable that the guidelines have been updated since then with more literature being published on important criteria. This made it difficult to compare NASS guidelines with ChatGPT’s generated responses. Additionally, ChatGPT version 3.5 is only able to pull data until 2021, also making it outdated. However, we adjusted for this limitation by comparing ChatGPT’s responses to the most recent literature to see if it aligned well with what is being published. Although we thoroughly graded ChatGPT’s responses, there exists the potential for subjective bias when determining the grading of each response. To mitigate this, we had 2 independent reviewers’ grade ChatGPT’s responses while a third reviewer resolved any discrepancies. Despite these constraints, we offer an evaluation of the effectiveness of 2 distinct ChatGPT models in delivering accurate recommendations for lumbar disc herniation with radiculopathy. CONCLUSION ChatGPT shows promising potential for its use in clinical settings. It was often able to provide useful information that was not included in the 2012 NASS guidelines. However, employing ChatGPT as a tool for clinical management should be done so with caution so as to ensure the safety and quality of care given to patients. Although ChatGPT can be used as a tool for answering medically relevant questions, physicians and healthcare workers should continue to refer back to relevant literature, published guidelines, and their own expertise when making clinical decisions. Finally, lay individuals attempting to replace medical consultations with ChatGPT’s outputs should also take considerable caution given that its responses are based on the quality of the questions being asked. As AI continues to evolve, further research needs to be performed to investigate its use in clinical settings.

documents.title: NASS evidence-based clinical guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of cervical radiculopathy from degenerative disorders

chunks.content: Introduction Cervical radiculopathy (CR) comprises mechanical compression, neuropraxia, or chemical irritation of the nerve roots, resulting in characteristic signs and symptoms of arm pain, paresthesia, arm muscle weakness, reduced deep tendon reflexes, and exacerbation of symptoms with neck movements. Radicular patterns of symptoms vary depending on the involved nerve root, although some distributional overlap may exist. The condition is more common in individuals aged 20 to 50 years and is considered a ‘clinical diagnosis with imaging confirmation’, which is most frequently performed with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). , The North American Spine Society clinical practice guidelines, recommend a careful evaluation of patient history and clinical signs and symptoms, as well as the judicious use of clinical tests such as shoulder abduction sign (e.g., Bakody’s test) and Spurling’s test. Past reviews have advocated similar tests. , However, considering the sensitivity and specificity of individual tests, authors reported limitations in using single test findings for diagnosis, a phenomenon known as “stand alone” weakness. Moreover, studies have reported that historical questions have poor diagnostic validity, justifying the use of validated combinations of physical tests to confirm the CR diagnosis. A past study built a clinical prediction rule (CPR), which combined test findings into a “single diagnostic test item cluster” to provide a more robust assessment of CR. The CPR included four tests: 1) upper limb neurodynamic test, 2) Spurling’s test, 3) cervical distraction, and 4) cervical rotation range of motion deficit on the side of radicular symptoms less than 60 degrees. To date, the CPR, which Wainner and colleagues published in 2003, has yet to be replicated and externally validated. There are three main stages in the development of CPRs: 1) derivation, 2) external validation, and 3) impact analysis to determine their influence on patient care. Within the external validation stage, both narrow and broad validations are advocated. Narrow validation involves replication in a similar clinical setting, using a similar population of patients. Broad validation comprises testing in widely variable clinical settings, in populations with varying degrees of disease severity and prevalence. A majority of derived CPRs never reach the validation phase, or fail validation when tested especially in unique patient populations. The objectives of our study were 1) to perform an independent broad validation of the 2003 CPR, using clinical examination and MRI as the reference standard and 2) to investigate whether a novel cluster of tests had a stronger diagnostic utility. We hypothesized that despite a difference in reference standards (the 2003 paper used electromyography as a reference standard), the CPR will still demonstrate strong diagnostic accuracy when discriminating CR and would represent the strongest cluster of tests evaluated. Methods Study design The study was a prospective diagnostic accuracy study with a consecutive cohort of patients presenting with neck pain and/or radicular symptoms (radicular pain, paresthesia, sensory or motor deficits) . All diagnostic decisions were made under conditions of diagnostic uncertainty. The non-CR group in our design represents individuals in which the clinician would differentially diagnose in a true given clinical setting. To improve the transparency of reporting, we followed the updated 2015 Standards for Reporting Diagnostic accuracy studies (STARD). The study was conducted in accordance with the ethical principles and the Helsinki Declaration on research involving human subjects and was approved (n°2212189v0). Participants Participants included consecutive patients presenting with neck pain and/or radicular symptoms, referred by a general practitioner or specialist between September 2017 and September 2019 to a Neurosurgery Department. This unfiltered recruitment approach was intended to reflect the clinical heterogeneity typically encountered in routine practice. All participants received the same diagnostic work-up, including an MRI, and were included for analysis ( ). Inclusion required reporting neck pain and/or arm pain of at least 3-months in duration, age 18 to 65 years, self-report of pain of at least 30 and less than 80 on a 100 mm visual analogue scale (VAS) , during the previous 24 hours, self-report of a score of ≥20 % on the Neck Disability Index questionnaire (NDI), , and symptoms of at least 3-months in duration. Potential subjects were excluded if they had suffered significant neck trauma at the time of the study, had a history of neck or arm surgery, inflammatory joint condition or arthritis, fibromyalgia, diabetes, psychiatric disorders, pregnancy, cardiovascular or neoplastic pathology, cervical myelopathy, pyramidal or extrapyramidal pathology, or were unable to speak or write in French. Test methods Index tests We analyzed 12 clinical tests or findings from the patient history in comparison to the diagnostic reference standard. No intervention occurred between the index test(s) and reference standard, which were performed on the same day. The clinical tests were the same as those previously studied by Wainner et al’s including all four upper limb neurodynamic tests (ULNT). The same physical therapist with 10 years of experience in neck pain management, and

arthritis, fibromyalgia, diabetes, psychiatric disorders, pregnancy, cardiovascular or neoplastic pathology, cervical myelopathy, pyramidal or extrapyramidal pathology, or were unable to speak or write in French. Test methods Index tests We analyzed 12 clinical tests or findings from the patient history in comparison to the diagnostic reference standard. No intervention occurred between the index test(s) and reference standard, which were performed on the same day. The clinical tests were the same as those previously studied by Wainner et al’s including all four upper limb neurodynamic tests (ULNT). The same physical therapist with 10 years of experience in neck pain management, and advanced certification for orthopedic assessment performed the clinical tests one hour after the clinical/MRI diagnosis. The physical therapist conducting the clinical tests was blinded to the patient's medical history and final diagnostic conclusions. Clinical tests included a modified shoulder abduction relief test (Bakody’s sign), performed passively by maintaining the patient’s hand on the head for 5 seconds to avoid pain from active execution (e.g., shoulder pain, apprehension). Spurling’s test with reproduction of familiar neck symptoms, Spurling’s test with reproduction of familiar arm symptoms. The cervical distraction test (∼14 kg for 10 s), and four upper limb neurodynamic tests (ULNT1, ULNT 2a, ULNT 2b, and ULNT3), with reproduction of familiar symptoms and structural differentiation, , cervical rotation <60°, neck range of motion ipsilateral<contralateral, age >48 years, duration of symptoms<62 weeks, which are described in the online material. The age and duration of symptoms cut offs were recommended after using area under the curve threshold assessments. Cut offs were determined with duration of symptoms <62 weeks, and age >48 years. Tests were considered positive or negative if they met the preset criteria (online material), and indeterminate if the patient was unable to tolerate the test position to allow test completion. Reference standard The diagnosis of CR or a competing diagnosis was made by a single neurosurgeon, who was masked to the results of the 12 clinical test findings (which occurred after the diagnosis and were not part of the neurosurgeon’s examination). The surgeon had 15 years of experience and based the diagnosis of CR on the following criteria: 1) history and presence of dermatomal radicular pain and/or symptoms (dysesthesia, sensory deficit, muscle weakness, or altered reflexes) attributable to a CR and 2) presence of MRI findings with nerve root compression or irritation due to disc herniation or foraminal stenosis at a relevant segmental level (i.e., the same or adjacent level) on the ipsilateral side consistent with the patient’s symptoms and neurological examination findings. Analysis Statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS version 26.0 Statistics for Windows, version 26 (IBM Corp., Armonk, N.Y., USA). Descriptive statistics were calculated as means and standard deviations (SD), frequencies, and percentages were tabulated to describe the included participants. Differences among those diagnosed with CR and those with competing conditions were evaluated with Wilcoxon rank-sum tests for continuous variables and chi-square or Fisher exact for categorical variables. All 12 clinical tests and the condition of 1 of 4, 2 of 4, 3 of 4, and 4 of 4 positive ULNT were individually examined for diagnostic accuracy against the MRI reference standard. Contingency tables (2 × 2) were used to calculate sensitivity and specificity, likelihood ratios (positive likelihood ratio [LR+]; negative likelihood ratio [LR−]), and posttest probabilities with a positive and negative finding for each single test. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves were used to determine all previously mentioned possible cut‐off values for age and symptoms duration. Sensitivity was defined as the proportion of individuals with cervical radiculopathy who had a positive test, while specificity was defined as the proportion of individuals without cervical radiculopathy who had a negative test. LR+ and LR− were calculated using the following formula: LR+ = sensitivity / (1 − specificity); LR− = (1 − sensitivity) / specificity. Post-test probability was calculated using Bayes’ theorem, based on the pre-test probability and LR: – Post-test probability with a positive finding = (pre-test probability × LR+) / [(pre-test × LR+) + (1 - pre-test)] – Post-test probability with a negative finding = (pre-test probability × LR-) / [(pre-test × LR-) + (1 - pre-test)] We ran two independent cluster analyses to test our two objectives. For our first objective (broad validation of the 2003 CPR), we included the same clinical tests (upper limb neurodynamic test, Spurling’s test, cervical distraction, and range of motion deficit to the side of symptoms less than 60 degrees) that were used by Wainner and colleagues. Using a similar strategy, we clustered the findings into conditions of 1 of 4, 2 of 4, 3 of 4, and 4 of 4 positive findings. Independent diagnostic accuracy values were run for each condition (e.g., 1 of 4, 2 of 4, etc. ). For our second objective (creation of a novel CPR), we identified the

our first objective (broad validation of the 2003 CPR), we included the same clinical tests (upper limb neurodynamic test, Spurling’s test, cervical distraction, and range of motion deficit to the side of symptoms less than 60 degrees) that were used by Wainner and colleagues. Using a similar strategy, we clustered the findings into conditions of 1 of 4, 2 of 4, 3 of 4, and 4 of 4 positive findings. Independent diagnostic accuracy values were run for each condition (e.g., 1 of 4, 2 of 4, etc. ). For our second objective (creation of a novel CPR), we identified the conditionally independent variables from the individual 2 × 2 analyses that yielded LR+ above 1.5 or LR− below 0.5 for a backward stepwise logistic regression analysis. This analysis was used to select variables, with p values of 0.15 to exit the model and 0.10 to enter it. This is a similar strategy to that used by Wainner and colleagues in 2003. Variables retained by the regression model were used to cluster findings and were then inputted into similar conditions (e.g., 1 of N, 2 of N, etc.). For each condition, sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative likelihood ratios, and post-test probabilities for both positive and negative findings were analyzed. Results Our study included 85 patients, including 31.7 % (n = 27) diagnosed with CR, whereas the non-CR group included 58 people, 42 of whom presented with neck without CR, 12 with peripheral nerve entrapment, and 4 with diffuse shoulder pain. The CR group presented with a significantly higher proportion of females and a longer duration of symptoms versus the non-CR group ( ). No adverse events from performing the index test or the reference standard were reported. The individual diagnostic accuracy values of our 12 pre-selected clinical tests are summarized in . The highest sensitivity was observed with one of the four ULNT tests, which had a sensitivity of 96.3 % and reached a post-test probability with a positive finding of 45.1 %. In contrast, the Spurling test demonstrated the highest specificity, with a positive likelihood ratio (LR+) of 34.37 (95 %CI = 4.80, 245.98) and a post-test probability with a positive finding of approximately 94.10 %. The strongest individual test for ruling out was cervical distraction, in which a negative test resulted in a post-test probability of 11.86 %. explores the broad validation of Wainner’s 2003 cluster, with the four following tests: 1) cervical distraction, 2) Spurling’s, 3) ULNT 1, and 4) cervical range of motion less than 60° to the ipsilateral side. Our findings show that the condition of 1 out of 4 positive tests was the most sensitive combination whereas the condition of 4 out of 4 four tests was the most specific. When none of the tests were positive, it ruled out all cases of CR (LR-=0.00; post-test probability = 0 %). The condition of having four out of four positive test results yielded an infinite LR+ and a post-test probability of 100% for confirming the diagnosis of cervical radiculopathy, however, having all four positive tests identified 17.9 % of patients with CR ( ). For our second objective, we evaluated an independent cluster using the test findings. Eight of the tests (shoulder abduction, cervical distraction, Spurling’s neck pain, Spurling’s arm pain, and the four ULNT) met our a priori criteria for inclusion in the backward stepwise regression. This analysis identified three variables that were included in the final model: 1) Modified shoulder abduction test, 2) Spurling’s arm pain test, and 3) 2 of 4 positive ULNT. The condition '2 out of 4 ULNTs’ was considered as a single composite variable, meaning any two positive results among the four described ULNTs. When none of the tests were positive, it ruled out all cases of CR (posttest probability=0 %). Having three out of three tests positive led to an infinite LR+ and a post-test probability of 100 % for confirming the diagnosis of cervical radiculopathy. When all three of the conditions were positive, no individuals without radiculopathy were identified as positive (post-test probability=100 %). Two of three positive tests yielded a LR+ of 7.06 (95 %CI=3.63, 12.20) and a LR- of 0.17 (95 %CI=0.06, 0.37) ( ). The study has been cited over 500 times but, to date, has not been independently (externally) validated in a separate study by a different authorship group. Since the 2003 publication, Wainner et al.’s clinical prediction rule for CR has been included in clinical practice guidelines, and is used frequently in clinical practice settings. The study has been cited over 500 times but, to date, has not been independently (externally) validated in a separate study by a different authorship group. Our study objectives were to 1) broadly validate the CR clinical prediction rule and 2) evaluate whether another rule was as effective or more effective than the 2003 rule created by Wainner and colleagues. We were able to accomplish both tasks. The broad validation of the 2003 CPR (Distraction, Spurling’s test, Ipsilateral cervical rotation <60°, and ULNT1), resulted in very similar diagnostic metrics for all categories. In fact, our results yielded a slightly better posttest probability with 2, 3, or 4 positive conditions (48.6 %, 78.2 %, and 100 %, respectively) compared to those reported by Wainner et al. (21 %, 65 %, and 90 %, respectively) ( ). Based on Wainner's test cluster, the probability increases to approximately 49 %, which is insufficient to establish a diagnosis. However, a diagnosis of cervical radiculopathy can be considered when at least three out of four tests are positive (78.2 %). Furthermore, when none of the four test findings were positive in our study, it completely ruled out the presence of CR (post-test probability=0 %). Wainner and colleagues did not report the LR- of their cluster nor did they calculate a post-test probability when none of the findings were present. Our results suggest that the CPR demonstrated both rule-in and rule-out utility when dedicated conditions (i.e., 1 of 4 versus 4 or 4) are evaluated. Whereas minor variations in diagnostic metrics are expected when examining a completely different study sample, we feel that other factors that are unique to our methodology are also worth reporting. For example, a positive test finding in our study for Spurling’s arm pain/symptoms test included reproduction of familiar arm signs or symptoms. Our results with a LR+ of 34.37 are consistent with previous studies reporting values between 6.75, 8.93, to infinity, particularly when peripheral radicular pain or symptoms were provoked. While Wainner and colleagues defined Spurling’s A as positive when symptoms were reproduced (either in the arm or the neck), we analyzed these two symptoms reproduction separately. Our results suggest that arm symptom reproduction has greater diagnostic value for cervical radiculopathy with radicular pain. Reproduction of familiar neck pain alone resulted in a poor LR+ (1.70) and posttest probability with a positive finding (44.1 %), which is also similar to past findings based on non-specific “symptoms reproduction” of the Spurling test, with LR+ ranging from 0.93, 2.1, to 6.75. Our definition of a positive ULNT test and the combined ULNT tests are also unique to our study. For those diagnosed with CR, we found that 85 % had 2 of 4 ULNT positive findings whereas 37 % of patients with CR had 3 of 4 ULNT positive findings. Previous evidence suggested that a fully negative ULNT profile is rare in patients with cervical radiculopathy and radicular symptoms, and no individual ULNT has demonstrated clear diagnostic superiority for CR diagnosis. In our study, the variable “≥2 ULNTs positive” — retained in the regression model — exhibited greater diagnostic utility than single ULNTs, particularly when interpreted alongside other clinical tests. Based on this finding, we would recommend the use of a ULNT cluster when assessing the potential for CR. To the best of our knowledge no previous published study assessed this condition of 2 of 4 ULNT positive findings in a cluster of tests for CR diagnosis. Our second objective was to explore whether a separate combination of findings led to a better diagnostic cluster than Wainner’s original tool. While our findings corroborate the original 2003 CPR, we also identified a new cluster that yielded slightly better post-test probability results than the replication of Wainner et al.'s CPR. Our best combination of tests incorporated: 1) the Modified shoulder abduction test, 2) Spurling’s arm pain test, and 3) at least two of four ULNT positive. As with the Wainner CPR, having all four tests negative rules out a CR diagnosis (post-test probability of 0 %). When all the tests were positive one is also able to rule in CR, with a post-test probability of 100 %. One potential benefit of our cluster, despite having to perform up to six tests (shoulder abduction, Spurlings’s, ULNT1, ULNT2a, ULNT2b, and ULNT3) versus four tests in Wainner’s cluster (range of motion, Spurlings’s, Distraction and ULNT1) is the number of individuals with CR that are correctly identified with our combination. Over 37 % of individuals with CR were captured when 3 of 3 conditions were positive in our study (100 % post-test probability), whereas only 17.9 % of with Wainner’s 4 of

the tests were positive one is also able to rule in CR, with a post-test probability of 100 %. One potential benefit of our cluster, despite having to perform up to six tests (shoulder abduction, Spurlings’s, ULNT1, ULNT2a, ULNT2b, and ULNT3) versus four tests in Wainner’s cluster (range of motion, Spurlings’s, Distraction and ULNT1) is the number of individuals with CR that are correctly identified with our combination. Over 37 % of individuals with CR were captured when 3 of 3 conditions were positive in our study (100 % post-test probability), whereas only 17.9 % of with Wainner’s 4 of 4 cluster (100 % post-test probability). This suggests that many subjects are missed in Wainner’s rule that are less likely misdiagnosed in our cluster. Although the Shoulder Abduction relief test (Bakody’s sign) has been commonly described in the past in CR diagnosis, , , few studies have assessed its diagnostic validity. Previous studies reported similar LR+ (Wainner 2.1; Sleijser-Koehorst 1.88; Viikari-Juntura 3.03; Gashemi 1.33). Previous studies reported sensitivities that have ranged from 17 % (Wainner) to 50 % (Sleijser-Koehorst) in comparison with 77.78 % in our study. The shoulder abduction test was performed differently in our study versus previous studies by Gashemi et al, Viikari-Juntura et al, Sleijser-Koehorst et al, and Wainner et al, as we had the examiner passively maintain the hand on the patient’s head for 5 seconds. This may be the reason for the increased sensitivity findings in our study, which influenced the combined modeling of multiple tests. Consideration needs to be given to the relative merit of clinical tests for relief and provocation of neck and arm symptoms. Some patients with CR may not have arm pain or symptoms at rest, hence achieving a reduction in symptoms is not possible during selected relief tests such as the neck distraction and shoulder abduction test. This might explain why relief of neck or arm symptoms are included as indicative of a positive test for both the Shoulder abduction test and Spurling’s test. This may also explain why tests evaluating symptom relief are more sensitive and provocation tests (Spurling‘s test and ULNT) were more specific. Further studies are necessary to investigate the accuracy of different criteria for positive tests in patients with CR with varying severity of neck and/or arm symptoms. The disparity in pre-test probability between our study (32 %) and Wainner's study (23 %) may be explained by differences in inclusion criteria (not detailed) and the use of EMG as the gold standard (versus clinical examination and MRI), which can yield negative results if performed before denervation or after complete reinnervation. We aimed to minimize pre-selection bias and reported a pre-test prevalence of CR (31.7 %) similar to that observed by Wainner et al. (23 %) in primary care settings. Although our novel cluster demonstrated clinically meaningful diagnostic performance — with a LR− < 0.1 (strong rule-out) when all tests were negative and an infinite LR+ (definitive rule-in) when all were Positive — post-test probabilities should always be interpreted within the clinical context. These values may differ in settings with higher pre-test prevalence, such as multidisciplinary referrals (49 %), or electrodiagnostic testing (79 %). A potential limitation of our study is the small sample size of 85 (including 27 people with CR), which may lead to less precision (e.g., wide confidence intervals). More impaired cases on the spectrum of CR might be represented in our sample. , The reference standard was determined by only one clinician while another evaluated all clinical tests. Although the clinical tester was blinded to the diagnosis of the patient, the transferability of their findings is unknown, since we did not test interrater agreement related to the index tests studied. This new cluster should also be interpreted with caution due to the regression model employed. Backwards stepwise regression method has the potential for unstable selection and overfitting. Further validation of this new cluster is required with a larger sample of patients with CR in diverse clinical settings (with no radicular pain, with posterolateral or foraminal or lateral recess radiculopathy), and larger non-CR group populations (cervicobrachial pain, thoracic outlet syndrome, etc. ), and with more examiner and reference standards including those evaluating nerve small fiber function and other forms of imaging such as magnetic resonance neurography. Conclusion Our findings broadly and independently validate the 2003 CPR for CR by Wainner and colleagues, and support its continued use in clinical practice. We were also able to identify a unique diagnostic cluster for CR with radicular pain that involved 1) a modified shoulder abduction test for arm pain relief, 2) Spurling’s test for arm symptoms provocation, and 3) at least 2 positive ULNTs. This new cluster ruled out all cases of CR when none of the tests were positive (post-test probability = 0 %) and it

fiber function and other forms of imaging such as magnetic resonance neurography. Conclusion Our findings broadly and independently validate the 2003 CPR for CR by Wainner and colleagues, and support its continued use in clinical practice. We were also able to identify a unique diagnostic cluster for CR with radicular pain that involved 1) a modified shoulder abduction test for arm pain relief, 2) Spurling’s test for arm symptoms provocation, and 3) at least 2 positive ULNTs. This new cluster ruled out all cases of CR when none of the tests were positive (post-test probability = 0 %) and it ruled in the CR diagnosis when two of three tests were positive (LR+ of 7.13 and post-test probability with a positive finding of 76.79 %). When all three criteria are positive the LR+ is infinite and post-test probability with a positive finding 100 %. Declaration of competing interest The authors declare no competing interest.

chunks.content: Research in context Evidence before this study We conducted an extensive literature review of PubMed employing keywords such as “osteoporosis”, “early warning”, “multiparameter data”, and “stacked ensemble model” to identify relevant studies published up to 20 March 2026, without language restrictions. The identified evidence was generally of moderate quality, with many studies limited by small sample sizes or a lack of external validation. Despite the comprehensive nature of this search, robust, clinically applicable findings were limited. Although existing research has explored the early diagnosis of osteoporosis, there remains a significant gap in the systematic integration of multidimensional serological models. This gap is especially pronounced in the development of specialised multiparameter stacked ensemble models tailored specifically for osteoporosis in women. Added value of this study This study identified 11 critical variables, including age, height, weight, and eight serum biomarkers associated with bone metabolism, blood lipids, and liver/kidney function. The OsteoSC-M3 model was developed and internally validated using a dataset comprising 5745 female participants from the National Centre for Orthopaedics at Shanghai Sixth People's Hospital, spanning the years 2013–2023. The model utilises a stacked ensemble framework, integrating nine base machine learning models with XGBoost serving as the meta-learner. It exhibited excellent diagnostic performance in both the Training and Internal Validation Sets, achieving area under the curve (AUC) values of 0.973 and 0.943, respectively. Decision curve analysis further confirmed its superior clinical utility compared to single-algorithm models. External validation conducted across two cohorts corroborated its exceptional diagnostic performance, with AUC values of 0.958 for Cohort 1 and 0.917 for Cohort 2. Prospective validation demonstrated strong concordance with follow-up results (Kappa = 0.82) and highlighted the model's capability to identify high-risk individuals for osteoporosis approximately 29 months before clinical diagnosis via traditional dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA), with significant predictive power (HR = 7.63, P < 0.001). The model significantly outperformed the Osteoporosis Self-Assessment Tool for Asians (OSTA) across all cohorts. Implications of all the available evidence The OsteoSC-M3 model developed in this study integrates demographic characteristics with eight straightforward laboratory parameters to facilitate early, non-invasive risk prediction of osteoporosis in women. It exhibits high diagnostic sensitivity and offers a clinical lead time of approximately 29 months. Surpassing OSTA in risk stratification, the model effectively identifies high-risk individuals who require DXA confirmation and is particularly suitable for settings with limited DXA resources. Additionally, we have launched a complementary online computing platform ( http://47.101.190.127:3838/scyz/ ), providing an innovative tool for early screening and intervention that aims to enhance participants' quality of life and reduce the burden on healthcare systems. Future research should focus on validating the model across diverse ethnic populations and assessing its long-term clinical impact through multicentre prospective trials. Introduction Osteoporosis is a systemic metabolic bone disorder characterised by reduced bone mass and the deterioration of bone microarchitecture. The fundamental pathological mechanism of osteoporosis involves an imbalance in bone remodelling, wherein osteoclast-mediated bone resorption surpasses osteoblast-mediated bone formation. , Globally, the prevalence of osteoporosis is estimated at 18.3%, with primary osteoporosis constituting over 90% of cases, predominantly encompassing postmenopausal and age-related osteoporosis. The incidence in women is two to three times higher than in men. In China, the disease burden among older adults is particularly pronounced, with a prevalence of 32.1% in women aged 50 and above, escalating to 51.6% in those over 65 years. The total number of women with osteoporosis is approximately 70 million, representing 77.8% of the national total of 90 million cases. , Osteoporosis can result in severe complications, such as osteoporotic fractures, which significantly impair quality of life and elevate the risk of disability and mortality among the elderly. , , Due to its long asymptomatic period and the lack of effective early screening tools, early diagnosis remains insufficient, resulting in high disability rates and substantial healthcare burdens. Therefore, developing convenient and reliable early screening methods for early detection and intervention has become a critical measure in addressing this public health challenge, with particular importance for safeguarding women's bone health. The current global diagnostic criteria for osteoporosis rely on DXA-measured bone mineral density or a history of fragility fractures. , , However, DXA presents significant limitations in early diagnosis: its two-dimensional projection cannot assess bone microstructure, exhibits low sensitivity to early metabolic changes, and faces accessibility barriers due to high costs and limited deployment (0.35 devices per million people in Asia; 3.7% testing rate among Chinese individuals aged ≥50). , , , Alternative methods include quantitative ultrasound with limited diagnostic efficacy, conventional CT with radiation concerns, and opportunistic CT with limited standardisation. Clinical risk assessment tools (e.g., ORAI, OSIRIS, SCORE) show pooled AUCs of 0.65–0.70, while FRAX, a fracture risk assessment tool, yields AUCs of 0.58–0.82. The IOF One–Minute Test and the Osteoporosis Self-Assessment Tool for Asians (OSTA) exhibit limited discriminative ability in Chinese populations, with AUCs of 0.629

to early metabolic changes, and faces accessibility barriers due to high costs and limited deployment (0.35 devices per million people in Asia; 3.7% testing rate among Chinese individuals aged ≥50). , , , Alternative methods include quantitative ultrasound with limited diagnostic efficacy, conventional CT with radiation concerns, and opportunistic CT with limited standardisation. Clinical risk assessment tools (e.g., ORAI, OSIRIS, SCORE) show pooled AUCs of 0.65–0.70, while FRAX, a fracture risk assessment tool, yields AUCs of 0.58–0.82. The IOF One–Minute Test and the Osteoporosis Self-Assessment Tool for Asians (OSTA) exhibit limited discriminative ability in Chinese populations, with AUCs of 0.629 and 0.798, respectively. These shortcomings in early diagnosis, radiation safety, and screening efficiency highlight the pressing need for the development of innovative screening methods. Osteoporosis is a dynamic pathological process primarily driven by an imbalance between bone resorption and bone formation. In clinical practice, circulating bone turnover markers and bone regulatory markers are commonly used to assess bone metabolism; studies have also reported that hepatic and renal function are closely associated with osteoporosis. , , Crucially, changes in these biomarkers precede radiologically detectable declines in bone mineral density, making it possible to assess early metabolic status before significant bone loss occurs. Relevant guidelines recommend incorporating routine blood tests—such as assessments of liver function, kidney function, blood lipids, and bone turnover markers—into the auxiliary diagnostic process, , , and affirm their importance in evaluating bone metabolism and predicting fracture risk, among other applications. However, due to significant overlap and variability in these biomarkers between healthy and osteoporotic populations, the diagnostic accuracy of individual markers is limited, necessitating multi-marker combined analysis to enhance diagnostic performance. , , Machine learning algorithms, excelling in processing high-dimensional data while reducing overfitting and enhancing interpretability, have become vital for complex disease diagnosis. , However, existing osteoporosis ML models based on serum biomarkers have notable limitations, including single-dimensional inputs, lack of sex-specific stratification, reliance on a single algorithm, and insufficient validation. , , Therefore, this study aimed to integrate multidimensional serological indicators and develop a stacked ensemble model for the early screening of osteoporosis in women. The model was validated through internal validation, multicentre external validation, and prospective cohort assessment, and was subsequently deployed as an open-access online platform to enable efficient risk stratification. Methods Study design and participant inclusion and exclusion criteria This study employed a multistage, multicentre observational cohort design ( ) to develop and validate a stacked multiparameter machine learning model for osteoporosis risk assessment. The analytical framework comprised five stages: model development, internal validation, external validation, prospective validation, and model interpretation with performance evaluation. This multicentre study was conducted at Shanghai Sixth People's Hospital in Shanghai and at Hai'an People's Hospital in Jiangsu Province, China. Participant sex was self-reported and extracted from electronic health records. Uniform inclusion and exclusion criteria were applied across all cohorts as follows: Inclusion criteria: (a) Han Chinese females; (b) aged 50–90 years; (c) underwent DXA bone mineral density examination or had a history of fragility fracture. Exclusion criteria: (a) menopausal status unknown; (b) long-term bedridden participants; (c) participants with severe cardiac, pulmonary, hepatic, renal, or haematological system diseases; (d) participants with endocrine, immune, or systemic metabolic diseases (e.g., type 1 diabetes, parathyroid disorders, osteogenesis imperfecta); (e) history of medication use including glucocorticoids, thyroid supplements, antidepressants, or anti-osteoporotic drugs; (f) comorbid malignancies, bone tumours, or history of bone metastases; (g) previous organ transplantation or history of lumbar spine/bilateral hip joint surgery. Cohort construction The model derivation cohort retrospectively enrolled females admitted to Shanghai Sixth People's Hospital between January 2013 and December 2023. Based on the inclusion and exclusion criteria, 5745 females were ultimately included from an initial pool of 32,066 individuals ( ). According to World Health Organization criteria and clinical guidelines, , participants were categorised into an osteoporosis group (T-score ≤ −2.5 by DXA or fragility fracture) and a non-osteoporosis group (T-score > −2.5 without fragility fracture). Fragility fractures were defined as low-energy trauma-induced (e.g., falls from standing height), excluding high-energy and pathological fractures. Fracture history was confirmed via electronic medical records and imaging reports, avoiding reliance on participant history alone. Vertebral fractures underwent DXA-based VFA per ISCD guidelines (T-score ≤ −1.0 or age ≥70 years ), with radiographic confirmation (Genant method: vertebral height reduction ≥20%). , This resulted in 2167 females (37.7%) in the osteoporosis group and 3578 females (62.3%) in the non-osteoporosis group ( ). To assess generalisability, two independent multicentre external validation cohorts were established. External Validation Cohort 1 consisted of 1839 females from Shanghai Sixth People's Hospital (January–December 2024), with 626 (34.04%) diagnosed with osteoporosis ( ). External Validation Cohort 2 included 305 females from Hai'an People's Hospital in Jiangsu Province, enrolled between January and June 2025, with 133 (43.61%) diagnosed with osteoporosis ( ). The baseline characteristics of both external validation cohorts were

radiographic confirmation (Genant method: vertebral height reduction ≥20%). , This resulted in 2167 females (37.7%) in the osteoporosis group and 3578 females (62.3%) in the non-osteoporosis group ( ). To assess generalisability, two independent multicentre external validation cohorts were established. External Validation Cohort 1 consisted of 1839 females from Shanghai Sixth People's Hospital (January–December 2024), with 626 (34.04%) diagnosed with osteoporosis ( ). External Validation Cohort 2 included 305 females from Hai'an People's Hospital in Jiangsu Province, enrolled between January and June 2025, with 133 (43.61%) diagnosed with osteoporosis ( ). The baseline characteristics of both external validation cohorts were comparable to those of the derivation cohort, as presented in . To assess the long-term predictive performance of the model, a Prospective Validation Cohort was established. This cohort, consisting of 405 female participants, was recruited from the Health Examination Centre of Shanghai Sixth People's Hospital between January 2015 and December 2019, which adhered to the inclusion and exclusion criteria detailed in Section . All participants presented with baseline osteopenia, characterised by a T-score ranging from −2.5 to −1.0, and none had osteoporosis at enrolment. They were prospectively followed until 31 December 2024, with a median follow-up period of at least five years. According to the Chinese osteoporosis and ISCD guidelines, , participants with low bone mass (T-score between −1.0 and −2.5) underwent DXA monitoring every 6–12 months to assess progression to osteoporosis. All participants underwent annual thoracolumbar radiography, with new fragility fractures assessed using electronic medical records, imaging reports, and radiographic findings. The baseline characteristics of this cohort are detailed in . DXA examination All dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) examinations in this study were conducted at the two collaborating institutions: Shanghai Sixth People's Hospital and Hai'an People's Hospital in Jiangsu Province. Measurements of bone mineral density at the lumbar spine (L1–L4), total hip, and femoral neck were performed by certified hospital technicians using Hologic Discovery Wi scanners (USA). Data were calculated using the US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES III) reference database, with the final diagnosis based on the lowest T-score among the three measurement sites. , Daily instrument calibration and quality control scans were routinely implemented to ensure data quality. Data collection and data cleaning In this study, we retrospectively collected demographic data and blood test results from female participants at their initial visit, synchronised with bone mineral density (BMD) assessments, encompassing a total of 35 clinically relevant parameters. The complete nomenclature is provided in . All laboratory data complied with ISO 15189 certification standards. Through a two-step data cleaning process, we first excluded five variables with a missingness rate exceeding 20% (β-CTX, CT, FT3, FT4, and TSH), followed by the removal of females with six or more missing parameters. After rigorous screening, we established a final dataset containing 5745 females and 30 parameters for subsequent imputation and analysis. This included four clinical features (age, height, weight, and BMI) and 26 blood biomarkers: 25-hydroxyvitamin D (VITD; ng/mL), total procollagen type I N-terminal propeptide (tP1NP; ng/mL), osteocalcin (OC; ng/mL), total cholesterol (CHOL; mmol/L), triglycerides (TG; mmol/L), high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDLC; mmol/L), low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDLC; mmol/L), potassium (K; mmol/L), sodium (Na; mmol/L), chloride (Cl; mmol/L), calcium (Ca; mmol/L), phosphorus (P; mmol/L), magnesium (Mg; mmol/L), total bilirubin (TBIL; μmol/L), direct bilirubin (DBIL; μmol/L), alkaline phosphatase (ALP; U/L), albumin (ALB; g/L), total protein (TP; g/L), alanine aminotransferase (ALT; U/L), gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT; U/L), aspartate aminotransferase (AST; U/L), cholinesterase (CHE; kU/L), total bile acids (TBA; μmol/L), prealbumin (PA; mg/L), uric acid (UA; μmol/L), and creatinine (CREA; μmol/L). Post hoc assessment of missing data mechanism To assess whether the missing data leading to sample exclusions can be considered missing at random (MAR), we conducted a missing indicator analysis. We constructed a post hoc multivariable logistic regression model with “exclusion due to six or more missing parameters” as the outcome and age, BMI, admission year, and osteoporosis diagnosis as covariates. The associations between missingness and observable variables were evaluated using odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) ( ). Laboratory testing According to standard hospital laboratory protocols for routine clinical testing, serum samples were prepared at room temperature by centrifugation at 3500× g for 10 min. Samples were stored at 4 °C and analysed within 4 h; aliquots were preserved at −80 °C for long-term storage. A Beckman AU5800 analyser (Beckman Coulter, USA) measured six electrolytes (K, Na, Cl, Ca, P, Mg), four blood lipids (CHOL, TG, HDLC, LDLC), eleven hepatic markers (TBIL, DBIL, ALP, ALB, TP, ALT, GGT, AST, CHE, TBA, PA), UA, and CREA. Serum tP1NP, OC, and VITD were quantified at Shanghai Sixth People's Hospital using a Roche Cobas E601 electrochemiluminescence system (Roche Diagnostics, Switzerland; reagent lots: 03141071190, 11972111122, 05894921190). Intra-assay and inter-assay coefficients of variation (CVs) were ≤3.0%/≤ 3.3%, ≤1.7%/≤ 3.3%, and ≤6.8%/≤ 8.5%, respectively. In Hai'an People's

Serum tP1NP, OC, and VITD were quantified at Shanghai Sixth People's Hospital using a Roche Cobas E601 electrochemiluminescence system (Roche Diagnostics, Switzerland; reagent lots: 03141071190, 11972111122, 05894921190). Intra-assay and inter-assay coefficients of variation (CVs) were ≤3.0%/≤ 3.3%, ≤1.7%/≤ 3.3%, and ≤6.8%/≤ 8.5%, respectively. In Hai'an People's Hospital (External Validation Cohort 2), these biomarkers were measured using a Snibe MAGLUMI X8 chemiluminescence analyser (Shenzhen New Industries Biomedical Engineering, China; reagent lots: 153240211, 088240121, 262250111), with intra-assay and inter-assay CVs ≤2.15%/≤ 2.50%, ≤1.61%/≤ 2.03%, and ≤1.65%/≤ 1.83%. All procedures followed manufacturer protocols. Statistical analysis All statistical analyses and data visualisations were performed using R (version 4.2.3), SPSS (version 22.0), MedCalc (version 20.2.1), and GraphPad Prism (version 10.4.0). Continuous variables are presented as mean ± SD (normally distributed) or median (IQR; non-normally distributed) to describe central tendency and dispersion; categorical variables are expressed as frequencies (%). Normality was assessed via the Shapiro–Wilk test (α = 0.05) with histogram/Q–Q plot verification to guide the selection of parametric or non-parametric tests. To compare continuous variables between cohorts, independent-samples t -tests were used for normally distributed variables with equal variances (Levene's tests); whilst Welch's t -tests were applied for unequal variances. Non-normally distributed variables were analysed using Mann–Whitney U tests. Categorical variables were compared via chi-squared or Fisher's exact tests based on expected cell counts; Kruskal–Wallis tests were utilised for comparisons involving more than two groups. Model performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves. Post hoc pairwise comparisons of the area under the curve (AUC) between models were performed using paired DeLong tests to determine statistical differences in diagnostic efficacy, with Bonferroni correction applied for multiple comparisons (α = 0.05; pROC package in R). Kaplan–Meier curves stratified by osteoporosis status depicted outcome variations, with hazard ratios (HRs; 95% CI) calculated using Cox proportional hazards regression models. All tests were two-tailed; P < 0.05 indicated statistical significance. Sample size estimation Sample size was determined based on the events per variable (EPV = 10) criterion, requiring a minimum of 110 osteoporosis events for the 11 variables under consideration. During the variable screening phase, a total of 4022 females from the Training Set, comprising 1526 osteoporosis (OP) cases and 2496 non-OP cases, were used for the preliminary assessment of 30 candidate variables. The Internal Validation Set included 1723 females, with 641 OP and 1082 non-OP cases. The validation phase involved three cohorts: External Validation Cohort 1, consisting of 1839 females (626 OP and 1213 non-OP); External Validation Cohort 2, comprising 305 females (133 OP and 172 non-OP); and a Prospective Validation Cohort of 405 females (154 incident OP and 251 non-OP), as illustrated in . All cohorts met the minimum statistical requirement of EPV ≥ 10, ensuring the robustness and generalisability of the model. Data partitioning and quality control To mitigate the risks of data leakage and model overfitting, the model derivation cohort including 5745 females was randomly partitioned into a Training Set (n = 4022) and an Internal Validation Set (n = 1723) at a ratio of 7:3. All data preprocessing parameters were determined exclusively on the Training Set and subsequently applied to both the internal and external validation cohorts to ensure unbiased model evaluation. The preprocessing pipeline consisted of three steps: As a post hoc sensitivity analysis, for samples with fewer than five missing parameters among the 30 retained variables, five imputation strategies (no imputation, MICE, KNN, median, random forest) were compared to determine optimal preprocessing ( ). Next, potential outliers in continuous variables were handled using median absolute deviation (MAD)-based winsorisation, with thresholds set at the median ±3 × MAD. Notably, a medical record review confirmed that specific outliers (n = 27) represented females with genuinely elevated tP1NP and OC levels, consistent with a diagnosis of accelerated bone turnover; therefore, these physiological values were exempted from winsorisation and retained. Finally, the impact of missing value imputation combined with four data transformation or scaling strategies was systematically evaluated: no transformation, log 10 transformation, standard (Z-score) scaling, and robust scaling. All analyses were performed in R 4.2.3. Performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and its 95% confidence interval on the Internal Validation Set. Variable selection Following missing value imputation, a multistage variable selection strategy was implemented on the complete dataset of 4022 Training Set females: first, variables with VIF>5 were excluded; subsequently, LASSO regression was employed, where the penalty coefficient λ was optimised via 10-fold cross-validation; finally, the selected variables were incorporated into a multivariable

Performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and its 95% confidence interval on the Internal Validation Set. Variable selection Following missing value imputation, a multistage variable selection strategy was implemented on the complete dataset of 4022 Training Set females: first, variables with VIF>5 were excluded; subsequently, LASSO regression was employed, where the penalty coefficient λ was optimised via 10-fold cross-validation; finally, the selected variables were incorporated into a multivariable stepwise logistic regression model with entry and removal criteria set at α = 0.05 and α = 0.1, respectively. Variable contributions were assessed using likelihood ratio tests, and adjusted odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals were calculated. Only independent predictors with P < 0.05 were retained in the final model. This strategy effectively reduced the risk of overfitting while ensuring the inclusion of clinically relevant and statistically robust variables. Construction of the OsteoSC-M3 stacked multiparameter machine learning model Model Framework: This study developed a two-level stacked ensemble framework to construct the Osteoporosis Serological-Clinical Multiparameter Intelligent Diagnostic Model (OsteoSC-M3), utilising Python 3.8 and R 4.2.3 with the tidymodels package. The base module incorporated nine parallel base classifiers ( , ): Random Forest (RF; random_forest (engine = "randomForest")), XGBoost (boost_tree (engine = "XGBoost")), Support Vector Machine (SVM; svm_rbf (engine = "kernlab")), Multilayer Perceptron (MLP; mlp (engine = "nnet")), Decision Tree (DT; decision_tree (engine = "rpart")), Logistic Regression (LR; logistic_reg (engine = "glm")), and three regularised models—LASSO (logistic_reg (mixture = 1, engine = "glmnet")), Ridge (logistic_reg (mixture = 0, engine = "glmnet")), and Elastic Net (ENet; logistic_reg (mixture = 0.5, engine = "glmnet")). Following independent predictions of the 11 key variables and the generation of output probabilities by each base classifier, the meta-module employed XGBoost as the meta-classifier. This meta-classifier was retrained using these probabilities as input features to produce the final osteoporosis (OP) prediction probability. The stacked architecture effectively amalgamates the strengths of diverse base classifiers, thereby enhancing predictive performance. For the stacked ensemble framework, the nine base classifiers were trained on the uniformly partitioned Training Set (70%) with hyperparameter optimisation via five-fold cross-validation and early stopping. The XGBoost meta-learner was subsequently trained using the out-of-fold (OOF) prediction probabilities generated by the base classifiers on the Training Set during the cross-validation process. To ensure comparability, model performance was comprehensively evaluated on the Internal Validation Set and two external cohorts using multiple metrics, including the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, negative/positive predictive values (NPV/PPV), F1 score, and Cohen's Kappa coefficient. Feature evaluation involved ranking variables by selection frequency across all models, with SHAP analysis generating swarm plots and case-specific interpretations to quantify feature importance and enhance decision-making interpretability. For model application, risk stratification using Youden's index categorised female participants into low- and high-risk osteoporosis groups, while Kaplan–Meier curves assessed prognostic associations with hazard ratios and 95% confidence intervals. Following multicentre external validation and prospective cohort assessment, the finalised model was deployed as an online platform that enables real-time osteoporosis risk evaluation through 11 key indicators, supporting early screening and risk stratification. Ethics statement The study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of the leading institution, the Sixth People's Hospital Affiliated to Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine (Approval No.: 2024-KY-277(K)), and this central approval was formally recognised by the Ethics Committee of Hai'an People's Hospital. The study was also registered with the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ChiCTR2500097213). This study included both retrospective multicentre cohorts and a prospective cohort, both utilising residual blood samples remaining after routine clinical tests. For the retrospective cohorts, data were retrospectively collected from electronic medical records by each participating centre, and the requirement for informed consent was waived by the ethics committees. For the prospective cohort, data were collected prospectively during clinical recruitment and follow-up, and all female participants in this cohort provided written informed consent. All data from the participating centres were anonymised locally prior to being aggregated and securely stored within the data management platform of Shanghai Sixth People's Hospital. This study adhered to the TRIPOD statement and STROBE guidelines. Results Study design and participants This study successfully established multiple independent cohorts for model development and validation ( ): (1) the Model Development and Internal Validation cohort (2013–2023) included 5745 females, randomly divided in a 7:3 ratio into a Training Set (n = 4022) and an Internal Validation Set (n = 1723); (2) multicentre external validation cohorts: External Validation Cohort 1 from Shanghai in 2024 (n = 1839) and External Validation Cohort 2 from Hai'an in 2025 (n = 305); and (3) a Shanghai Prospective cohort (2015–2019, n = 405), which enrolled female participants with baseline osteopenia but without osteoporosis and followed them for at least five years. All cohorts were independent and non-overlapping. A five-stage framework was employed as follows: a stacked machine learning model was developed using the Training Set; preliminary validation was performed internally; external validation was conducted across two centres; long-term predictive performance was evaluated using the prospective cohort; an optimal threshold was determined based on Youden's index to generate the computer-based model OsteoSC-M3 for stratifying high- and low-risk populations; finally, the performance of OsteoSC-M3 and the Osteoporosis Self-Assessment Tool for Asians (OSTA) was compared using clinically confirmed osteoporosis as the reference standard, and the SHAP algorithm was applied to interpret feature importance and non-linear interactions. Baseline analysis of the derivation cohort In this baseline analysis, we examined 5745 females from the model derivation cohort, consisting of 2167 females diagnosed with osteoporosis (OP) and 3578 non-osteoporosis (Non-OP) controls. Appropriate statistical tests were conducted to compare baseline characteristics at initial admission, including demographic variables (age, height, weight) and 26 serum biomarkers ( ). The statistical analysis indicated that the OP group was significantly older and had higher levels of tP1NP, OC, HDLC, TBIL, DBIL, ALP, TBA, and Mg in comparison to the Non-OP group (all P < 0.05). In contrast, the OP group exhibited significantly lower levels of BMI, VITD, CHOL, TG, LDLC, ALT, GGT, CHE, PA, UA, and CREA (all P < 0.05). These results imply that the differentially distributed serum biomarkers are closely associated with the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying osteoporosis. Data partitioning and variable screening To mitigate the risk of data leakage and model overfitting, the model derivation cohort comprising 5745 females was randomly partitioned into a Training Set (70%, n = 4022) and an Internal Validation Set (30%, n = 1723) at a 7:3 ratio. Analysis of missing data for the 30 parameters in the Training Set revealed an overall data completeness of 93% with a missingness rate of 7% ( ), indicating acceptable data quality for subsequent analysis. Random forest imputation without transformation yielded the optimal performance for females with fewer than five missing parameters ( , ). Following data preprocessing, a multistage variable selection strategy was implemented on the complete Training Set of 4022 females. First, multicollinearity was assessed using the variance inflation factor (VIF) analysis ( ), leading to the exclusion of body mass index (BMI) due to its high collinearity with height and weight. Subsequently, redundant variables were eliminated via LASSO regression ( A). This comprehensive screening procedure identified 11 key predictive variables from the initial 30 features, including three demographic characteristics (age, height, weight) and eight serum biomarkers (VITD, tP1NP, OC, CHOL, TBIL, DBIL, ALP, UA) ( ). Multivariable logistic regression confirmed that all 11 variables were significantly associated with osteoporosis, with five identified as independent risk factors (age, tP1NP, OC, TBIL, ALP) and six as independent protective factors (height, weight, VITD, DBIL, CHOL, UA) ( B). Area under the curve (AUC) analysis demonstrated limited diagnostic efficacy of individual variables for osteoporosis, with AUC values ranging from 0.563 to 0.703 ( ). Base module construction and performance evaluation During model training, osteoporosis cases were designated as the positive class, while non-osteoporosis controls constituted the negative class. Based on the 11 key variables identified through variable selection, we developed base models using nine machine learning algorithms—including RF, XGBoost, SVM, MLP, DT, Logistic Regression, Ridge, ENet, and LASSO ( ). To ensure comparability of model performance, all models were constructed and optimised using the same 4022 training females from the model derivation cohort, and internally validated with 1723 internal validation females. The missing data pattern in the Internal Validation Set is shown in , and missing values were imputed using the pre-trained missForest model derived from the Training Set ( ). As illustrated in , all nine base models demonstrated strong performance, with AUC values ranging from 0.84 to 0.95 on the Training Set (

To ensure comparability of model performance, all models were constructed and optimised using the same 4022 training females from the model derivation cohort, and internally validated with 1723 internal validation females. The missing data pattern in the Internal Validation Set is shown in , and missing values were imputed using the pre-trained missForest model derived from the Training Set ( ). As illustrated in , all nine base models demonstrated strong performance, with AUC values ranging from 0.84 to 0.95 on the Training Set ( A, ) and from 0.83 to 0.91 on the Internal Validation Set ( C, ). Further comparison revealed minimal differences (0.003–0.04) in AUC between the training and validation sets for each model, indicating stable performance without significant fluctuations or overfitting ( B and D; ). Nevertheless, the absolute AUC values of individual models still left room for improvement, suggesting a direction for subsequent optimisation. Construction and internal validation performance of the stacked ensemble model OsteoSC-M3 Variable importance analysis revealed notable dependencies on predictive variables across nine distinct algorithms ( ), justifying the ensemble learning strategy. We implemented a stacking approach where base models generated independent probability predictions based on the 11 key variables, which were then used as features to develop an XGBoost meta-model. Using 5745 females split 7:3 for training and validation, this two-tiered architecture effectively integrated complementary strengths of diverse algorithms, significantly enhancing generalisation capability and predictive accuracy. As shown in , the XGBoost-based meta-module, OsteoSC-M3, demonstrated robust and stable performance in both the Training Set (AUC 0.973, 95% CI 0.969–0.976; sensitivity 91.1%; specificity 92.5%) and the Internal Validation Set (AUC 0.943, 95% CI 0.933–0.954; sensitivity 86.6%; specificity 89.1%) ( A, ). The PR curve further indicated that OsteoSC-M3 maintained stable performance in both the Training Set (AUPRC 0.956) and the Internal Validation Set (AUPRC 0.908) ( B). In addition, decision curve analysis (DCA) showed superior clinical utility, as reflected by the stable and consistent areas under the DCA curve across both cohorts ( C and D). In summary, the OsteoSC-M3 intelligent early-warning model for osteoporosis exhibits strong and consistent performance across both the Training and Internal Validation Sets, suggesting its potential as a reliable tool for osteoporosis risk stratification. Performance evaluation of OsteoSC-M3 in multicentre external validation To evaluate the robustness and generalisability of OsteoSC-M3 across varied clinical environments, we conducted external validation at two independent medical centres located in distinct geographical locations: the National Centre for Orthopaedics at Shanghai Sixth People's Hospital and Hai'an People's Hospital in Jiangsu. Validation Cohort 1 consisted of 1839 females from the National Centre for Orthopaedics at Shanghai Sixth People's Hospital (2024; 626 cases of osteoporosis and 1213 non-osteoporosis controls). In contrast, Cohort 2 comprised 305 females from Hai'an People's Hospital, with 133 cases of osteoporosis and 172 controls. The missing data status of the 11 core variables comprising the OsteoSC-M3 model within External Validation Cohort 1 (n = 1839) is presented in , with missing values imputed using the pre-trained missForest model derived from the Training Set. Meanwhile, these 11 core variables demonstrated 100% data completeness in External Validation Cohort 2. Detailed baseline characteristics are provided in . In Cohort 1 ( A and ), OsteoSC-M3 exhibited excellent performance, with an AUC of 0.958 (95% CI 0.949–0.966), sensitivity of 88.7%, and specificity of 86.4%. Although slightly lower performance metrics were observed in Cohort 2 ( B and )—with an AUC of 0.917 (95% CI 0.897–0.928), sensitivity of 84.5%, and specificity of 86.6%—all metrics exceeded 85%, thereby confirming the robust cross-centre stability of OsteoSC-M3. Furthermore, OsteoSC-M3 exhibited excellent calibration between predicted and observed risks ( C and D). Moreover, decision curve analysis (DCA) corroborated its superior clinical utility across various centres ( E and F). This consistency highlights the model's significant potential for early prediction of osteoporosis in diverse clinical settings. Interpretability and feature importance analysis of OsteoSC-M3 The predictive contributions of the 11 key features (age, height, weight, and eight serum biomarkers) in the OsteoSC-M3 model were systematically elucidated through SHAP analysis ( A). B presents the comprehensive computational workflow of OsteoSC-M3, which incorporates nine foundational models, as demonstrated through a specific case study. As shown in C, the risk stratification visualisation using a red-blue colour gradient (red indicating high-probability outputs from base models, blue indicating low-probability outputs), combined with SHAP value quantification, clarified the significant contributions of these base learners to the overall ensemble prediction of osteoporosis. Further evaluation of the importance distribution across nine base modules ( ) revealed that random forest, XGBoost, and SVM demonstrated the most prominent contributions, followed by the DT model ( D), providing critical insights into the decision-making mechanism of the ensemble model.
