Further evaluation of the importance distribution across nine base modules ( ) revealed that random forest, XGBoost, and SVM demonstrated the most prominent contributions, followed by the DT model ( D), providing critical insights into the decision-making mechanism of the ensemble model. Prognostic value analysis and online computing platform for OsteoSC-M3 To evaluate the clinical utility of OsteoSC-M3 for early diagnosis and progression monitoring of osteoporosis, we conducted a prospective cohort study of 405 participants with confirmed low bone mass (T-score between −2.5 and −1.0) who did not initially have osteoporosis. The follow-up period spanned a minimum of five years, with the primary endpoint being the development of osteoporosis. The mean interval between DXA tests was 12.39 ± 3.11 months. Baseline data are available in . During the follow-up, 154 females (38.02%) developed osteoporosis, with 12 new fragility fractures identified (8 vertebral and 4 hip fractures). The 11 core variables maintained 100% data completeness in the Prospective Validation Cohort. The OsteoSC-M3 model generated predicted outcomes using the participants' initial diagnostic data, and a comparative analysis of these predictions against actual outcomes is depicted in the confusion matrix ( A). The model's risk stratification, utilising an optimal cutoff threshold of 0.40, effectively categorised females into high-risk (≥0.40) and low-risk (<0.40) groups, demonstrating substantial agreement with actual diagnoses (Kappa = 0.82) ( ). Furthermore, there was strong calibration between observed outcomes and the OsteoSC-M3 scores ( B). The model provided risk alerts approximately 29 ± 9.31 months earlier than DXA detection ( ), with longitudinal analysis revealing significantly higher predictive values for females who progressed to osteoporosis ( ). Kaplan–Meier analysis indicated significantly higher osteoporosis incidence in the high-risk group (HR = 7.63, P < 0.001) ( C). The web-based OsteoSC-M3 platform ( http://47.101.190.127:3838/scyz/ ) integrates demographic and eight biochemical parameters to generate individualised reports ( ), enabling rapid quantitative evaluation through its user-friendly interface and establishing a closed-loop management system for osteoporosis screening, diagnosis and intervention. Performance comparison between OsteoSC-M3 and OSTA, and subgroup analysis This study systematically compared the newly developed OsteoSC-M3 model with the widely used Osteoporosis Self-Assessment Tool for Asians (OSTA). While OSTA calculates risk based solely on age and weight, OsteoSC-M3 integrates height and eight routine serological biomarkers related to osteoporosis pathogenesis (in addition to age and weight). Performance comparison across multiple independent cohorts ( ) demonstrated consistent superiority of OsteoSC-M3 in terms of area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC): Training Set (0.973 vs 0.720), Internal Validation Set (0.943 vs 0.739), External Validation Cohort 1 (0.958 vs 0.726), and External Validation Cohort 2 (0.917 vs 0.613). We also compared the AUC of OsteoSC-M3 with the other models and found that it significantly outperformed all other models across all cohorts ( ). These findings underscore the critical value of incorporating multidimensional clinical indicators for enhanced osteoporosis diagnostic performance. To validate the robustness of the OsteoSC-M3 model, we performed a post hoc subgroup analysis on 1526 females in the osteoporosis group of the Training Set ( ): the AUC difference between the Low BMD and fracture history subgroups was 0.014 (0.975 vs 0.961; P = 0.16). Post hoc sensitivity analysis showed that after removing females with a fracture history, the model AUC increased only slightly by 0.002 (from 0.973 to 0.975) ( P = 0.25), confirming that the heterogeneity of the osteoporosis group did not have a clinically significant impact on model performance, and the model is robust and reliable. Discussion The ageing population has made osteoporosis a major concern, significantly impacting the quality of life for older adults. , In China, women represent 77.8% (70 million) of osteoporosis cases, particularly postmenopausal and elderly women. Early diagnosis and intervention are crucial for preventing fractures and improving quality of life. , , , , , To address this, we developed OsteoSC-M3, a machine learning model that combines age, height, weight, and eight serum biomarkers. It was developed and internally validated with 5745 females from Shanghai Sixth People's Hospital and further tested on two independent multicentre cohorts of 1839 females from Shanghai and 305 females from Hai'an, as well as a prospective osteopenia cohort. The model outperformed single-modal algorithms, enabling non-invasive risk stratification approximately 29 months before clinical diagnosis. An online platform has been created for dynamic assessment, aiming to proactively improve screening strategies. This approach is expected to enable early intervention, significantly enhancing participants' quality of life and reducing healthcare costs. This approach is expected to enable early intervention, significantly enhancing participants' quality of life and reducing healthcare costs. Based on the pathogenesis of bone remodelling imbalance (initiated by osteoclast-driven bone loss and amplified by hepatorenal dysfunction) , and the observation that serum biomarkers (tP1NP, OC, blood lipids, and renal parameters) precede DXA-detectable BMD reduction, , we developed the OsteoSC-M3 model. This model integrates 11 variables—five risk (age, tP1NP, OC, TBIL, ALP) and six protective factors (height, weight, VITD, DBIL, CHOL, UA)—reflecting three core pathophysiological pathways: metabolic–bone axis disruption, oxidative stress, and remodelling imbalance. Elevated bone formation markers (tP1NP, OC, ALP) indicate accelerated turnover and increased fracture risk, while vitamin D exerts protective effects via calcium absorption and bone homeostasis. Although cholesterol (CHOL) can increase risk via oxidative stress/inflammation-mediated osteogenesis inhibition and osteoclastogenesis, it emerged as a protective factor in our study, potentially reflecting better overall nutritional status in this ageing cohort. Uric acid (UA) protects bone in non-gout populations (consistent with this gout-free cohort). , Bilirubin shows biphasic effects: normal levels protect via antioxidants, but pathological elevation accelerates osteoporosis, , , with TBIL/DBIL exhibiting metabolic state-dependent divergence. These findings confirm osteoporosis as a localised manifestation of systemic metabolic dysregulation. SHAP analysis and case-specific visualisation validated model interpretability ( , ). Constructed with a stacked ensemble framework, the model demonstrated excellent internal validation performance ( A) and superior efficacy vs single-algorithm models, with multicentre external validation yielding AUCs of 0.958 (Cohort 1) and 0.917 (Cohort 2). Prospective validation showed prediction 29 months earlier than clinical diagnosis. The stacking mechanism enables dynamic fusion of base model advantages through meta-learning, accommodating multistage pathogenesis. Missing data analysis confirmed robustness (AUC fluctuation<0.02 post-imputation; ). The deployed online platform ( http://47.101.190.127:3838/scyz /) facilitates early screening and dynamic risk assessment. Multicentre validation demonstrated that OsteoSC-M3 maintained excellent performance in both cohorts, though Cohort 2 showed a moderate decline (AUC 0.917) compared to Cohort 1 (AUC 0.958). Systematic feature analysis revealed: (1) population heterogeneity in demographic parameters; (2) consistent detection systems for five internationally traceable biomarkers; and (3) platform/methodological differences in tP1NP, OC, and VITD measurements (Roche ECLIA in Cohort 1 vs Snibe CLIA in Cohort 2). The observed performance variations primarily stemmed from methodological heterogeneity and population characteristics. Notably, both external validation cohorts demonstrated excellent diagnostic performance ( ), robustly confirming OsteoSC-M3's cross-platform and cross-centre generalisability. To further enhance adaptability, future studies could employ feature-alignment transfer learning to optimise decision weights for platform–sensitive parameters, combined with locally weighted learning for regional model fine-tuning, thereby balancing architectural stability with improved generalisability. This study evaluated the novel OsteoSC-M3 model for osteoporosis screening vs the widely used OSTA tool. While OSTA showed better discriminative ability (AUC 0.798) in Chinese populations than other clinical tools, , OsteoSC-M3 demonstrated significantly superior performance across all validation cohorts: Training Set (AUC 0.973), Internal Validation Set (AUC 0.943), External Validation Cohort 1 (AUC 0.958), and External Validation Cohort 2 (AUC 0.917)—substantially exceeding OSTA's results (0.720, 0.739, 0.726, 0.613) ( ). These consistent findings confirm OsteoSC-M3's enhanced discriminatory power and underscore the value of integrating osteoporosis-relevant serological biomarkers to improve screening accuracy and generalisability. This study demonstrates two key innovations: the OsteoSC-M3 machine learning model identifies predictive factors through multiparameter interaction analysis, enhancing clinical interpretability, and the tool provides simple, accurate continuous risk prediction, enabling early risk alerts months before DXA confirmation. Limitations include: binary classification requires expansion to a ternary system (normal/osteopenia/osteoporosis); lifestyle factors and genetic markers remain unincorporated; and model development relied on single-centre data from East China, with validation limited to Asian females aged ≥50 years. Crucially, clinical accessibility of certain laboratory parameters may be limited in smaller hospitals or resource-constrained regions where these data are not routinely collected. Furthermore, while fracture history was documented, the potential for silent fractures to be overlooked when relying on medical records may introduce diagnostic bias. Future multicentre studies should validate generalisability in broader populations (including males and younger women), with risk assessment refined by incorporating comprehensive fracture imaging. Importantly, this model aims to optimise DXA resource allocation through preventive early warning in large-scale primary screening, not to replace clinical diagnosis. In conclusion, the OsteoSC-M3 model, which integrates demographic information and eight serological laboratory parameters, enables the early prediction of osteoporosis in women (approximately 29 months before clinical diagnosis).
